title: Duplicates and keys
story:
A duplicate is not a repeated row. It is two rows that refer to the same thing, and those are different problems with different solutions, only one of which is a single function call.

The underlying idea is old and precise. Codd's relational model, published in 1970 in Communications of the ACM, puts relations into a normal form in which each one carries a designated primary key — the field, or combination of fields, that identifies the thing rather than the record. Its opening argument is data independence: users of a large data bank should be protected from having to know how it is organised internally, so that applications survive changes to the representation. A key is what makes that possible, because it gives you a way to refer to an entity that does not depend on where the entity is stored or how many times it has been written down.

Real collected data frequently has no such field. Two systems each generated their own identifiers, or the entity is a person and the only handles you have are a name, an address and a date. At that point comparison stops being the right operation, because the records that refer to the same person are not equal and never will be — one has a middle initial, one has an old address, one has a typo.

That problem was formalised in 1969, by Fellegi and Sunter in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, building on Newcombe's earlier approach from 1959. Their framing is the one to carry: comparing a pair of records is a decision with three possible outcomes, not two — link, non-link, and possible link — and the optimal procedure is a likelihood ratio test which minimises the number of pairs left undecided while holding two error rates at levels you stipulate. Those two errors are linking records that do not match, and failing to link records that do.

Notice what that structure admits. There is no threshold that removes both errors; tightening against one loosens the other, and the third outcome exists because some pairs genuinely should be sent to a human rather than decided. So the honest question is not how accurate the matching is, but which of the two mistakes you would rather make — and that is a question about consequences, not about data. Merging two customers who are different people and merging two records for one person fail in opposite directions, and only you know which is worse in your setting.

problem.name: Entity resolution
problem.shape: You need to count or join things, and the table contains records — several of which may refer to the same thing without being identical.
tell: two systems each supplied their own identifiers for the same entities
the only handles on an entity are a name, an address or a date
a total does not reconcile after exact duplicates have been removed
the join key is something a human typed
problem.move: Establish the key before counting anything. Where the data carries one, assert its uniqueness so that a violation stops the pipeline. Where it does not, treat matching as a decision with three outcomes rather than two, set the two error rates deliberately from the consequences, and route the undecided band to a person instead of pretending the threshold settled it.
problem.invariant: A key identifies the entity rather than the record. Counting things is only arithmetic when such a field exists; otherwise every count is the output of a matching decision, whether or not anyone made that decision consciously.
problem.breaks: Natural keys are the ones that break, because they are attributes rather than identifiers: an email address changes hands, a phone number is reassigned, a name changes, an address is updated between two captures. The field keeps working as a key right up until the entity it describes changes, and then it silently identifies the wrong thing.

cost.time: a uniqueness assertion is one check; probabilistic matching is a modelling exercise plus a human review queue that does not go away
cost.space: a resolved identifier column mapping records to entities, kept alongside the source identifiers rather than replacing them
cost.beats: exact deduplication alone, which removes the duplicates that were already identical and leaves every one that matters, while making the table look as though the problem has been handled

worked.problem: Dropping exact duplicates removed twelve rows, and your totals still do not reconcile. Why?
worked.reasoning:
Because exact deduplication answers a question about records, and reconciliation asks a question about things.

Dropping exact duplicates removes rows that are identical in every compared field. That catches the mechanical duplicates — a file loaded twice, a retry that committed, a union that overlapped — and those are real and worth removing. It is also the easy fraction, and it leaves the population of interest untouched.

The duplicates that spoil a total are the ones that are not identical. The same person with a middle initial in one row and not the other. A trailing space, a different capitalisation, an address that was updated between the two captures, a timestamp that differs by a second because the two systems recorded different moments. Every one of those pairs refers to one thing and compares as two, and no exact method will ever see them.

Underneath that is the real issue: without a key, you were never counting things. You were counting records and hoping the two numbers agreed. A key is the designated identifier for the entity rather than the row, and where the data has one, reconciliation is arithmetic. Where it does not, matching is a decision problem.

Treated as a decision problem it has known structure. Each pair of records resolves to a link, a non-link, or a possible link, and the optimal rule is a likelihood ratio test that minimises how many pairs are left in the middle while holding two error rates at stipulated levels — linking records that do not match, and failing to link records that do. The third outcome is not a hedge; it is where the pairs go that should be looked at by a person.

Which means the question to bring back is not how accurate the matching is. It is which of the two errors is more expensive here. Over-merging makes two different customers into one and silently deletes a person from your counts; under-merging makes one customer into two and inflates them. Those fail in opposite directions, and nothing in the data tells you which is worse — that comes from what the numbers are for.

problem.practice: Take a table you believe has a key and assert that the key is unique — if the assertion fails, you have found something. Then take a table with names or addresses in it, normalise case and whitespace, and count how many new duplicate pairs appear that exact comparison had missed. Write down, before you set any threshold, which of the two errors you would rather make and why.

beats.broke: Two rows can describe the same thing without being the same row, so the number of distinct things in a table is not the number of rows and cannot be recovered by testing rows for equality.
beats.fix: Declare a key — the field that identifies the thing rather than the record, which is what the relational model put into normal form in 1970 — and where no such field exists, treat matching as a decision with three outcomes and two stipulated error rates, as formalised in 1969.
beats.cost: Exact comparison finds only the duplicates that were already identical, and every probabilistic method trades its two errors against each other. No threshold removes both, so the real choice is which mistake you would rather make.

interview.q: Dropping exact duplicates removed twelve rows, and your totals still do not reconcile. Why?
interview.trap: Loosening the comparison until the numbers agree — normalising more fields, lowering a threshold — which is choosing an error rate by whether the answer looks right, rather than from what the two mistakes cost.
interview.answer:
Because exact deduplication answers a question about records, and reconciliation asks a question about things.

Dropping exact duplicates removes rows identical in every compared field. That catches the mechanical cases — a file loaded twice, a retry that committed, an overlapping union — which are real and worth removing, and which are also the easy fraction.

The duplicates that break a total are the ones that are not identical. The same person with a middle initial in one row and not the other, a trailing space, a different capitalisation, an address updated between two captures, timestamps a second apart because two systems recorded different moments. Each pair refers to one thing and compares as two, and no exact method will find them.

The deeper problem is that without a key you were never counting things at all — you were counting records and hoping the numbers agreed. A key identifies the entity rather than the row, which is what makes counting arithmetic. Where there is no key, matching becomes a decision problem.

As a decision problem it has known structure: every pair resolves to a link, a non-link, or a possible link, and the optimal rule is a likelihood ratio test that minimises how many pairs sit in the middle band while holding two stipulated error rates — linking records that do not match, and failing to link records that do. The third category is not indecision, it is the queue for human review.

So the question I would take back is not how accurate the matching is. It is which error is more expensive here. Over-merging makes two customers into one and quietly removes a person from the counts; under-merging makes one customer into two and inflates them. They fail in opposite directions, no threshold eliminates both, and nothing in the data can tell you which is worse — that depends on what the numbers are being used for.

WHEN THERE IS NO KEY

   the records for one person are not equal
   and never will be.

   comparison is the wrong operation.
   matching is a decision, formalised 1969:

      link  |  non-link  |  POSSIBLE link
                             ^ send to a human

      optimal = likelihood ratio test
      holding two error rates you STIPULATE

THE TRADE YOU CANNOT ESCAPE

        over-merge  <--------->  under-merge
     a person vanishes        counts inflate

   no threshold removes both.
   pick the error you would rather make,
   on consequences, not on data.

THE QUESTION TO ASK FIRST

   not "are there duplicates"
   but "what is the key, and if there isn't one,
        which mistake is cheaper?"
takeaway: A duplicate is two rows referring to one thing, not a repeated row — so without a key you are counting records rather than entities, and once matching becomes a decision no threshold removes both errors, leaving you to choose which mistake is cheaper.
